title: Noach: whole-hearted (Genesis 6:9)
hook: the portion opens by calling Noah tamim, whole

segments.voice: Yesterday, Enoch, who walked with God, and the end of the first portion. Your line was walk with God. Did you take the slow walk? Today, a new portion: Noach. Day one hundred sixty-six.

Lunch eaten while answering email. A friend heard while half-reading a text. A show watched while scrolling another screen. A lot of life gets done with part of ourselves, and the rest somewhere else. And then there are the other moments, done with all of a person. Holding a newborn. Playing music. A conversation so good the time disappears. The second portion of the Torah describes its hero with a Hebrew word for exactly that. Today's word.
screen: `LUNCH, EMAIL, ANOTHER SCREEN.` → `A MOMENT WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD FOR A WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Noach, Noah, and it begins: "These are the generations of Noah. Noah was in his generations a man righteous and whole-hearted; Noah walked with God." There's yesterday's phrase again: walked with God. And there's today's word. Whole-hearted, in Hebrew, is tamim. It means whole, complete, without a crack. The same word describes an animal fit for an offering: unblemished, nothing missing. Later, God tells Abraham, walk before me and be tamim. And Moses tells the people, "Thou shalt be whole-hearted with the LORD thy God." It's not a word for perfect, as in never making mistakes. It's a word for undivided. All of you, in one place. Then the rabbis notice two small words: in his generations. Why add that? The Talmud records a disagreement. One teacher says it's praise: if Noah was righteous even in a violent generation, imagine what he'd have been in a good one. Another says it's a limit: righteous for his generation; in Abraham's time, he wouldn't have stood out. Rashi quotes both, and doesn't choose. The Torah gives Noah a grand word, and the rabbis ask you to think about it from two sides. Either way, the text sets Noah's wholeness in a world that was coming apart. The verses right after say the earth was filled with violence. In the middle of that, one person was undivided. That's what tamim asks. Not perfection. Wholeness, in whatever generation you're in.
screen: `NOAH WAS RIGHTEOUS AND WHOLE-HEARTED.` · `TAMIM: WHOLE, WITHOUT A CRACK.` · `NOT PERFECT. UNDIVIDED.` · `IN HIS GENERATIONS: PRAISE OR LIMIT?` · then, large: `WHOLE-HEARTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be in one place. Settle, and breathe. Notice where the parts of you are: some in this room, some in a worry about tomorrow, some in a conversation from yesterday. Gently call each part back, one at a time, like calling people to the table. Now be here, all of you, for one breath. Then another. If a part wanders off, call it back without scolding. The bell holds the time.
Tamim. Whole, complete, undivided: the word the Torah uses for Noah, and for being whole-hearted with God.
Your line: whole-hearted. Today, do one ordinary thing with all of you: a meal, a conversation, washing a dish, with nothing else open. Day one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Parashat Noach, Genesis 6:9–11:32, is read on the second Shabbat after Simchat Torah; teachers often begin with the debate over 'in his generations' in Rashi and the Talmud.

as a limit: only righteous compared to his time.
fork.reveal: the Talmud records both readings, and Rashi quotes both without choosing.

trapdoor: what you thought: Noah was perfect.
what it means: Noah was whole, undivided, in a world coming apart; and the rabbis ask whether 'in his generations' praises or limits him.
what a scholar hears: Sanhedrin 108a (Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish) on 'bedorotav'; tamim of sacrifices (Leviticus 22:21); Genesis 17:1 and Deuteronomy 18:13.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 6:9 and Deuteronomy 18:13.

Sanhedrin 108a: Rabbi Yochanan (compared to Abraham he would be nothing) and Resh Lakish (all the more in a righteous generation). Confirm which teacher holds which view; the script leaves them unnamed.
Genesis 17:1 paraphrased ('walk before me and be tamim').
Tamim for unblemished offerings (e.g. Leviticus 22:21): confirm.
